1 · Summary of conclusions

Terms. Claws beyond E[claws | boutons]: z-scored claw similarity minus its least-squares fit from z-scored bouton similarity across the 136 pairs (a residual; the same construction for somata, models and other references). Its odor part is the additive fit ai + aj, with one odor value ai per odor; the pair part is the rest. Figure labels and CSV columns use the names odor effect (odor value), pair-specific (pair part) and claw_beyond_boutons.

Bottom line

  1. KC claws carry KC-soma-like odor structure beyond their PN-bouton input from the first reliable time point. Holding bouton similarity fixed, claw similarity tracks KC-somata similarity (+0.475, p = 0.0001). The somata were recorded in other flies. The component is already present at 0.5–1 s, stays flat through the odor, and is what somata inherit: predicting somata from both, claws carry the weight (+0.81) and boutons add little (+0.13). All of this holds with the 4-fly kc_remy somata matrix too, with effects about 15–20% smaller (+0.396, p = 0.0002; §3.10).
  2. That structure is connectome-like. The hemibrain wiring model also predicts it (+0.30, p = 0.003). Random wiring, ORN input, chemistry (ECFP) and natural sources (VCF) don't.
  3. There is no slow "ORN-like → somata-like" handover in claws when fixed (static) ORN and KC-somata reference matrices are used. Claws are closer to somata than to ORNs at every frame where their matrix is reliable (Spearman Δρ +0.07 to +0.15).
    • Figure 7F's somata side replicates in all 4 flies, but it rests on one frame (t = 0.5 s).
    • That frame is coarse and globally correlated, and the cluster score partly reflects how many clusters each matrix gets.
    • Boutons score just as "somata-like" by that metric.
  4. The main change over time is fast decorrelation. A broad onset response decorrelates within about 0.5 s in both boutons and claws, about twice as much in claws. Bouton geometry also drifts toward ORNs during the odor.
  5. Which pairs move, and when (§3.8). The largest claw–bouton movers mostly preview the somata: 9 of the top 10 move the same way there, and claws pull somata-cluster partners together from 0.5 s. About a third of the reshaping is in the odor part (linalool, aa, IaA and 2h pulled toward the other odors; the alcohols, B-cit, ep and ms pushed away); only this part carries the hemibrain-specific connectivity bias, during the sustained odor. The stable pair part is predicted by either connectivity model, not by their difference (§3.8.1); the difference's pair part is concentrated in the partners of 2-but, aa and 1-8ol, and claws could follow it (reliability ceiling 0.78) but mostly don't (§3.8.3). The reshaping is non-uniform in time: stable from 1 to 3 s, different at onset and after offset, with odor-specific timing that survives kinetic and compression controls.
  6. APL model. Delayed APL inhibition fits the extra decorrelation in claws. It isn't needed for, and isn't supported as the cause of, the somata-like geometry. The model's slow spike-trace handover doesn't match the timing. The slow change that does exist is in the odor part (§3.8).
  7. Data provenance.
    • The claw files don't record their ROI mask.
    • The Figure 7 folder's files are byte-identical to those analyzed.
    • The PN-bouton timeseries are the 5-fly PN-bouton set; Figure 6 and Table 1 use 6. Decision: report n = 5 for the Figure 7 boutons.

3 · What was done and what it showed

3.1 The timeseries and the dashboard

The PN-bouton files were read first: their layout, the stim vs trial matrices, and per-fly within-odor and between-odor time courses. An interactive dashboard was then built to reproduce Jonathan's 17 × 17 grid of correlation time courses. It was later extended with the KC-claw files and a Difference view: PN boutons − KC claws, with the area between the curve and zero filled by whichever region is higher.

  • Controls: region (PN boutons, KC claws, or difference) and its direction; stim or blockavg matrix; z-scored or raw traces; for claws, neuropil-corrected Fc or uncorrected F; fly or fly mean; r or 1 − r; full matrix or one triangle; and odor selection, reordering and clustering.
  • Resampling: PN boutons (0.2 s frames) are interpolated per fly onto the claws' 0.25 s frames before differencing.
  • Exports: PNG, SVG and CSV.
  • Accuracy: in-page values match an independent Python calculation within 2 × 10⁻⁵.
  • Access: a private web copy is at claude.ai/artifact/JRq4FC9c3N4wAVcABp3LHP. An offline copy is outputs/reports/correlation_timeseries_dashboard.html.

First look (first_look_window_means.csv): averaged over the 136 odor pairs, the two regions' between-odor correlations are nearly equal. The differences are specific to odor pairs.

3.2 Is the PN-bouton − KC-claw difference real?

Each odor appears in 16 of the 136 pairs, so significance comes from shuffling odor labels rather than treating pairs as independent. Logs: code/logs/diff_structure.log and followups.log.

  • The pair pattern replicates across independent flies. The PN-bouton − KC-claw difference computed from disjoint fly halves (PN-bouton 2|3 × KC-claw 2|2, 30 splits) correlates at r = +0.49 across pairs (p ≤ 0.0005). This holds in every window.
    • The part of claw similarity not linearly predicted by boutons also replicates (r = +0.57), so it isn't just compression.
  • Compression: during the odor, KC-claw r ≈ 0.80 × PN-bouton r (0.54× after offset). Rank agreement between the regions' matrices is ρ = 0.72 during the odor.
    • Part of the compression is measurement noise (added October 19). Trial-to-trial noise is uncorrelated between trials, so it shrinks every observed r by the geometric mean of the two regions' reliabilities (observed r = true r × √(reli·relj); same-odor single-trial reliability over 0.5–3 s: boutons 0.71, claws 0.64). Correcting both regions moves the single-trial slope of claw r on bouton r from 0.77 to 0.85 over 0.5–3 s; by window, 0.72 → 0.77 (0.5–1 s), 0.81 → 0.87 (1–2 s), 0.75 → 0.86 (2–3 s) and 0.55 → 0.59 (after offset). So roughly a third of the apparent compression is noise and two thirds is real. The pattern of which pairs differ is untouched (raw vs corrected agree at r = 0.99 for both regions), so every pair-level result below is unaffected; only the compression magnitude changes. Table: 2_claw_vs_bouton_differences/compression_disattenuated.csv.
  • Pairs and odors (5 vs 4 flies; Welch t test with BH correction):
    • No single pair survives q < 0.05. Three pass q < 0.10: IaA–Lin, t2h–va and 1-6ol–t2h. 19 pairs reach p < 0.05, against about 7 expected by chance.
    • Linalool stands out: its mean r with other odors is 0.125 in boutons and 0.243 in claws.
  • Not organized by chemical class (alcohol, ester, ketone, aldehyde, acid): p = 0.45.

3.3 What the claw–bouton differences track

Method. For each reference matrix, the standardized partial coefficient in claws ~ boutons + reference (136 odor pairs, fly means).
  • PN-bouton noise: bouton noise would otherwise leak into the reference's coefficient. To prevent that, boutons from one half of the PN-bouton flies are predicted by the other half (two-stage least squares), averaged over all 20 half-splits.
  • Calibration: in simulation the test stays near 0 when claws simply inherit boutons, where a plain regression does not (code/checks/sim_iv.py).
  • p-values: permutation of odor labels (Freedman–Lane).
  • Error bars: leave-one-odor-out jackknife.

  • Somata. The somata effect survives:
    • dropping any single odor (0.34–0.52);
    • adding a curved (quadratic) bouton term (+0.38, p = 0.001);
    • using ranks (+0.45).
    Predicting somata from both compartments gives claws +0.81 (p = 0.0005) and boutons +0.13 (p = 0.48). The KC-stage reorganization is therefore visible from the boutons → claws step.
    • More similar in claws: linalool pairs (2h–Lin, IaA–Lin, Lin–aa, B-cit–Lin), plus t2h–va and IaA–pa.
    • Less similar in claws: mostly alcohol pairs.
  • Hemibrain vs somata. In a joint model somata keep their weight (+0.42, p = 0.0002) and the hemibrain model adds little (+0.13, p = 0.16).
  • ORN. There's no sign that claws undo or extend the ORN → bouton changes. ORN and bouton matrices are nearly collinear (r = 0.83), though, so only large effects are excluded.
  • Natural sources. VCF structure doesn't change from boutons to claws; it enters from claws to somata (+0.21 ± 0.10, p = 0.0008).
    • That holds for every embedding with 3 or more dimensions (+0.08 to +0.21).
    • It vanishes with raw VCF distances (+0.006), the same embedding dependence noted for Figure 6.
  • Over time (0.5 s bins):
    • The somata component is +0.49 at 0.5–1 s and stays at 0.43–0.47 through 3 s.
    • Just after offset (3.25–4.25 s) it is +0.65 (p = 0.0002). That's higher than during the odor, but not significantly (+0.17 ± 0.19).
    • After offset, claws also keep chemical (ECFP) structure that boutons lose (+0.35, p = 0.0005). The simplest reading is slower claw kinetics.

3.4 Figure 7E/F cluster check

This repeats the Figure 7 procedure on these files.

  • Clustering: each fly's window matrix is clustered by average linkage, with the number of clusters k chosen by silhouette (k ≤ 7).
  • Comparison: the clusters are compared with the ORN and KC-somata clusters by adjusted Rand index (ARI).
  • Windows: early [0.5, 0.75) s, which is a single claw frame, and late [1.5, 2.0) s.
  • Reference clusterings:
    • ORN (k = 2): benz + ms vs the other 15 odors.
    • KC somata (k = 6): {2h, IaA, pa}, {2-but, eb, ep}, {1-8ol, B-cit, Lin}, {1-5ol, 1-6ol, 6al, t2h, benz}, {aa, va}, {ms}.
Claw flyk early → lateARI vs ORNARI vs KC somata
1 (2023-04-11/2)5 → 4+0.22 → +0.20+0.12 → +0.27
2 (2023-04-11/3)2 → 7−0.12 → +0.07+0.04 → +0.62
3 (2023-04-13/1)3 → 7+0.28 → +0.07+0.17 → +0.44
4 (2023-04-15/2)2 → 7+0.59 (chance level) → +0.02−0.03 → +0.46
  • Somata side replicates: agreement rises in 4/4 flies (mean 0.07 → 0.45), and the rise survives resampling trials within each fly (P ≥ 0.94 per fly).
  • ORN side is weaker:
    • Agreement falls in 3/4 flies, and only 2/4 are above chance early.
    • The fall survives trial resampling in only 1 fly.
    • Trial-averaged (blockavg) matrices show ORN agreement rising in 3/4 flies.
  • What drives it:
    • At t = 0.5 s, claw clusterings are coarse: one big group plus outliers. One frame later (0.75 s) the somata groups appear, ARI vs somata is already 0.44, and it stays there.
    • The 0.5 s frame isn't noisy (split-half reliability 0.80), but its odors are broadly correlated (mean r 0.38).
    • By rank correlation it is already closer to somata (0.71) than to ORN (0.60).
  • Number of clusters matters. ARI rewards partitions of similar granularity: ORN's silhouette choice is k = 2, somata's k = 6, early claws pick 2–5 and late claws 7.
    • With claws and both references cut at the same k, the somata rise holds at every k (2–7). The ORN fall appears only at k = 5–7.
    • At k = 5–7, the early → late shift toward somata relative to ORN is +0.27 in claws vs ≤ +0.08 in boutons. That is the clearest claw-specific cluster effect.
  • Boutons as a control: boutons agree with the somata clusters as well as late claws do (0.42 → 0.52), even though they are the most ORN-like stage by rank correlation.

3.7 Interpretation against the APL (delayed-inhibition) model

The model write-up in this folder is delayed-inhibition-model-sketch.md, with overview.html; it comes from another session. It assumes:

  • delayed APL feedback (τ_A ≈ 0.6 s);
  • a slow spike-associated claw calcium component (τ_BP ≈ 1.8 s);
  • steady bouton input.

Under those assumptions the model predicts early input-like claws that become somata-like over seconds.

Model assumption or predictionWhat the data showVerdict
Boutons hold; claw dynamics are generated in the calyxBoutons decorrelate with a similar time course, and their rank geometry drifts toward ORNnot supported
Delayed APL (τ ≈ 0.6 s) decorrelates clawsClaw decorrelation on a ~0.5 s scale, about 2× the boutons'consistent for the extra claw decorrelation. Decorrelation changes the level, not rank geometry
Early claws input-like; a slow spike trace unmasked by inhibition makes late claws somata-like (model Δρ −0.09 → −0.05, crossing zero at 4.2 s)Somata-like component present at 0.5 s and flat to 3 s; Δρ +0.11 / +0.15 early → +0.07not supported
A claw can't change rank geometry with its own input alone (each claw a monotone function of its input), so KC-level information is neededClaws differ from boutons in a somata- and hemibrain-like way from 0.5 sopen The step to "KC-level signal" assumes claws and GH146 boutons weight glomeruli alike, and that claw ROIs exclude somata. The model samples glomeruli uniformly
Most somata-like just after offset+0.65 vs about 0.48 during the odor (not significant); claw signals outlast boutonstrend only

Conclusion. The KC-stage reorganization of odor geometry is present in claw signals from the first reliable frame, doesn't build up over the odor, and is passed on to somata. Delayed APL inhibition can account for the extra claw decorrelation, but not for the somata-like rank structure. The open mechanistic question is which of two explanations holds:

  • (a) KC-level signal in claw calcium. It would have to be fast, not a 1.8 s accumulating trace.
  • (b) Claw-local sampling. Claws may sample glomeruli differently from the imaged GH146 boutons (GH146 labels about 70% of PNs, and the connectome over- and under-samples glomeruli).

Discriminating tests:

  • a claw-only ROI mask;
  • in the connectome model, a claw-input readout without KC thresholding vs the KC-output readout;
  • blocking KC output (Kir/shibire);
  • APL silencing, which should remove the extra claw decorrelation.

3.8 Which pairs move most, and when

Question. What is the significance of the odor pairs that move most between boutons and claws, and is the reshaping of claw relationships uniform over time?

Approach. "Moving" is measured after removing the overall compression. In each window, claw similarity is z-scored across the 136 pairs, and the part predicted linearly by same-time bouton similarity is subtracted. This is "claws beyond E[claws | boutons]", in SD units; positive means more similar in claws than the boutons predict.

  • The pattern is computed from fly-disjoint halves (PN-bouton 2|3 × KC-claw 2|2, 30 splits) to measure reproducibility.
  • An additive model splits it into an odor part (each odor's general pull toward, or away from, all other odors) and a pair part.
  • p-values come from odor-label permutation.
  • Windows: 0.5–1, 1–2 and 2–3 s, and 3.25–4.5 s after offset.

Answer in brief

  • The movers are real, and most of them preview the KC somata.
    • The pattern replicates across fly halves in every window (split-half r 0.56–0.60).
    • 9 of the 10 largest movers move the same way in KC somata, which were recorded in other flies.
    • The pair part matches somata beyond E[somata | boutons] in every window (r 0.65–0.71, p < 0.001).
    • Claws pull together the odors the somata group. Within- minus between-cluster pairs: +0.40 SD for the whole pattern and +0.49 for the pair part (0.5–3 s; p ≤ 0.007 in every window).
  • About a third is in the odor part.
    • Pulled toward the other odors: linalool (+0.62), aa (+0.34), IaA (+0.28) and 2h (+0.27).
    • Pushed away: 1-6ol (−0.32), 1-5ol and ep (−0.24), B-cit (−0.23), 1-8ol (−0.19) and ms (−0.15).
    • This is the only part that carries the hemibrain-specific bias. It matches the hemibrain-minus-uniform difference during the sustained odor (r 0.54 at 1–2 s, p 0.02; 0.62 at 2–3 s, p 0.008), not at onset (0.21) or after offset (0.17). The pair part never does (r 0.13–0.16, p 0.07–0.15), yet it is predicted by each connectivity model on its own (see §3.8.1).
    • It isn't a reliability artifact: disattenuated single-trial similarity gives the same odor values (r 0.95–0.97).
  • The reshaping is non-uniform in time, and reproducibly so.
    • The pattern is stable from 1 to 3 s (noise-corrected stability 0.97). It differs at onset (0.5–1 vs 2–3 s: 0.78 ± 0.09) and after offset (0.56–0.76).
    • The early → late change replicates across fly halves (r 0.46, p 0.001) and is 62% odor part.
    • The timing is odor-specific. Linalool's pull is largest at onset and fades, and aa's builds. t2h, ep and ms separate progressively. B-cit, 6al, va and benz start distinct and relax.
  • During the odor, it isn't a kinetics or compression artifact.
    • Claws match same-time boutons best; no lag improves the fit.
    • The change survives lagged, low-passed and multi-lag bouton predictors and quadratic or rank fits (split-half r 0.34–0.50, all p ≤ 0.001). It is unrelated to bouton similarity (r −0.05).
    • After offset, claws match boutons from about 0.75 s earlier, so post-offset changes are partly kinetic.

Largest movers, 0.5–3 s. In each of these, the two fly halves agree in sign in at least 29 of the 30 splits.

Boutons r and claws r are fly-mean correlations at 0.5–3 s. Cluster letters are as in the §3.4 figure.

  • Linalool and created similarity. Three of the five biggest gains involve linalool. Four of the top six are pairs that PN boutons keep nearly uncorrelated (r ≈ 0.1 or less) but claws bring to r 0.24–0.38. This similarity is created at the PN-bouton→KC-claw step and is also present in the somata.
  • Losses. Four of the five largest losses separate an alcohol (1-5ol, 1-6ol or 1-8ol) from B-cit, va, ep or t2h.
  • Pair part effects. The largest are t2h–va (+1.66), 1-5ol–1-6ol (+1.25; somata +2.40), 2-but–ep (+1.19) and IaA–pa (+1.01). Three of these four are somata-cluster partners.

Interpretation. The two parts behave differently over time.

  • Pair part. The somata-like reorganization is present from 0.5 s and changes least: it carries 38% of the early → late change.
  • Odor part. This is what evolves: which odors are broadly pulled together or pushed apart, on odor-specific time courses.

Three mechanisms would produce this odor-part timing, and these data can't tell them apart:

  • APL feedback scaled by each odor's KC drive (a delayed, activity-dependent process acting per odor);
  • KC-intrinsic inhibition such as mAChR-A;
  • glomerular input dynamics that aren't visible in GH146 boutons.

Relative to §3.7: a slow component does exist, but it acts on the odor part, not on the somata-like pair structure. Two tests follow:

  • Correlate each odor's change with its KC drive (e.g. its coding level in the somata).
  • If APL is responsible, silencing it should flatten the odor-specific timing and leave the pair part.

3.8.1 Which part follows the connectivity models?

Question (Jonathan, October 18). The hemibrain and uniform models differ only in connectivity, which does not change in time; so shouldn't the part of the reshaping that is present throughout, the pair part, be the one that matches hemibrain minus uniform?

Answer. The premise is right: the pair part is the stable one (noise-corrected stability 0.91–0.98 across the odor windows; the odor part's early-to-late stability is 0.50). And it is connectivity-driven. But it follows what the two models share, not their difference. Each model's similarity was residualized on same-window bouton similarity, exactly as the claw pattern is, and split into odor and pair parts (alignment_by_model_window.csv):

WindowHemibrain modelUniform modelHemibrain − uniformKC somata
0.5–1 s0.29 (p 0.003)0.23 (p 0.013)0.14 (p 0.14)0.65 (p 0.0002)
1–2 s0.32 (p 0.001)0.26 (p 0.005)0.14 (p 0.13)0.68 (p 0.0002)
2–3 s0.37 (p 0.0004)0.31 (p 0.001)0.14 (p 0.15)0.71 (p 0.0002)
3.25–4.5 s0.47 (p 0.0002)0.42 (p 0.0002)0.16 (p 0.07)0.65 (p 0.0002)

Pair part of claws beyond E[claws | boutons] vs the pair part of each reference beyond E[reference | boutons]; odor-label permutation, two-sided.

  • The stable pair-part reshaping is a generic PN-bouton→KC-claw effect. Both models predict it, hemibrain only slightly better (by about 0.06). Their pair-part predictions overlap (r 0.58 with each other, 0.48 and 0.40 with the somata), and subtracting one from the other removes exactly the shared part the claws follow.
  • The hemibrain bias shows up only at the odor level. The model difference is not purely an odor part (64% of its variance is in the pair part), but the claws do not follow that pair part. What they follow is which odors the biased wiring pulls toward, or pushes away from, all the others: in the model, benz (+0.50), Lin (+0.43) and va (+0.38) up; 2-but, 1-5ol and eb (−0.25 to −0.29) down.
  • Static wiring need not give a static match. A fixed connectivity bias shapes the RDM only through whichever PNs are active and how strongly, which changes over the response, and the model predictions come from a single response per odor. The onset→sustained rise in the odor-part match is not itself significant (change vs model difference r 0.38, p 0.14); the drop after offset is (r −0.50, p 0.04). With 17 odor values per window, the safer statement is that the bias signature is clearest during the sustained odor and gone after offset, not that it is absent at onset.

In terms of the population vectors. An odor-part shift means one odor's response vector moves toward or away from the whole odor cloud, by gaining or losing a component along the axis the population shares, or by a change in its reliability. A pair-part shift means two odors gain claws that respond to both and to little else: a shared private subspace, which is what a set of KCs sampling glomeruli common to both odors produces, in any wiring scheme. A somata cluster is the same thing for a group of odors.

3.8.2 Scale and linearity of the fit

Question (October 18). Is regressing correlations on correlations valid, and why Pearson rather than Spearman?

  • Bounded scale. All fly-mean r lie in [−0.06, 0.78], where Fisher's z is nearly linear; on the z scale the pattern correlates 0.99 with the reported one.
  • Dependence between pairs. The 136 pairs share odors, so parametric OLS p-values would be wrong. Every p here is an odor-label permutation, and reproducibility is measured across disjoint flies.
  • Noise in the predictor. Bouton r is itself noisy; the split-fly IV (§3.2) handles this for the somata coefficient.
  • Linearity. This is the one real caveat. The claw-vs-bouton relation at 0.5–3 s is convex (quadratic term F = 27.8, p < 0.001; a cubic adds nothing): claws separate middling-similarity pairs more than the extremes, and the linear residual averages +0.08 / −0.16 / +0.03 across bouton-similarity terciles (r 0.36 with bouton z²). This convexity is a real feature of the PN-bouton→KC-claw transform (a sparsening nonlinearity produces it), so the linear residual is not wrong, but the paper should say the relation is convex.
  • Pearson vs Spearman. Claws and boutons are the same kind of measurement, so magnitudes are comparable, the slope is the compression, and the residual has interpretable units; a rank transform discards that. For the model RDMs, whose scale is arbitrary, Spearman is the usual choice, and §3.5 already reports both r and ρ. In practice the choice moves nothing (table).

3.8.3 What is in the hemibrain − uniform difference, and why claws follow only part of it

Question (Jonathan, October 19; run on the Mac against the local data). §3.8.1 found that the claws' pair-part reshaping follows what the two connectivity models share, not their difference. What does the difference consist of, and is the lack of pair-level following a power problem?

  • What the difference is. The two model RDMs correlate at r 0.85. The difference (SD 0.55, z units) is 36% odor part (benz +0.50, Lin +0.43 and va +0.38 pulled toward the other odors; 2-but, 1-5ol, eb and ep pushed away) and 64% pair part.
  • The pair part is concentrated. Its ten largest pairs carry 48% of its variance and the twenty largest 69% (an even spread: 7% and 15%). Three odors dominate: the bias re-sorts the partners of 2-but (toward aa +1.48, eb, ep; away from 6al −1.11, t2h, benz), aa (toward 2-but, B-cit +1.00, ep; away from va −1.32, benz) and 1-8ol (toward t2h +1.41, 6al; away from ep, eb −1.00). It is not a curvature of the uniform model (a quadratic of uniform adds 0.02 R²; r 0.08 with uniform's pair part), and it is not organized by somata clusters (+0.16, p 0.14) or chemical class (+0.06, p 0.52).
  • Not a power problem. The claw pair part's split-half reliability is 0.59–0.63 in every window, so its correlation ceiling against a noiseless predictor is ≈ 0.78. The somata reach 0.69; the model difference reaches 0.13–0.16 (disattenuated 0.17–0.21). A trace is present: the partial correlation given the uniform model's pair part is 0.16–0.22, significant only at 2–3 s (p 0.048) and after offset (p 0.022); on the 20 largest-difference pairs claws agree in sign on 14 and the somata on 12; on the 15 pairs the bias pushes up or down most, claws move +0.11 / −0.18 and the somata +0.21 / −0.28. The somata follow the difference a little (r 0.20, p 0.03), mostly on the 2-but/aa/1-8ol pairs (r 0.30).
  • What the bias adds as a predictor of claws. Claws beyond E[claws | boutons] ~ uniform beyond E[uniform | boutons]: R² 0.05; adding the difference: R² 0.16 (ΔR² 0.11, p 0.001). Split by level, the gain is almost all in the odor part: for the 17 odor values R² rises from 0.02 to 0.46 (p 0.005), while the pair-level gain is the small partial above.
  • Model input. The uniform model's RDM is essentially the ORN RDM (r 0.97), whereas measured boutons differ from ORN (r 0.87): both models were driven by ORN-like input, so the difference is the bias applied to ORN responses. The pair-level mismatch between the uniform model and measured boutons does not predict where the difference is large (r −0.04), so this does not explain the weak following; but the pair-level predictions for aa, 2-but and 1-8ol rest on those odors' ORN responses rather than on what the boutons carry.

In one sentence

The hemibrain-specific bias appears in claws as a re-weighting of which odors are broadly similar, not as the specific partner re-sorting of 2-but, aa and 1-8ol it predicts at the pair level; the claws' pair-part structure is the part either wiring scheme produces.

Script: code/analysis/model_difference_characterization.py (run with python3 -E on the Mac; paths from code/paths.py). Outputs in outputs/results/9_model_difference/.

3.9 Data provenance checks

  • ROI mask. The claw files contain no record of which ROI mask was used: no cell_mask_coord, attribute or string, and the YAML lists only suite2p paths. Figure 7's panel text says iscell_calyx, but the region name is kc_claws_and_soma. This should be confirmed in the pipeline.
  • File identity. The four NetCDFs in data/rdm_timeseries/ have SHA-256 hashes identical to the files analyzed, so re-running on them would give identical numbers. If they are the Figure 7 inputs, the differences from the Figure 7 draft come from analysis choices, not data.
  • PN-bouton fly set. The PN-bouton timeseries are the newer 5-fly PN-bouton set, which drops the downsampled acquisition 2022-10-21/2. Figure 6 and Table 1 use the 6-fly set.
    • The match to the distance table's columns shows this: r = 0.98 with Figure 6's pn_boutons_F_zscore, and r = 0.998 with new_pn_boutons_zscore.

3.10 Robustness to the KC-somata reference

Question (October 16). Do the results hold with kc_remy instead of kc_remy_combo?

  • kc_remy comes from the 4 flies imaged in 2022: all 17 odors and the highest-quality data. It is identical to the table's new_kc_soma_nls_zscore.
  • kc_remy_combo (used everywhere above) adds 14 flies from 2018–19 with partial panels (5–16 odors; aa is missing from nearly all of them).
  • How they differ. The two matrices correlate at r = 0.97 (ρ = 0.94).
    • They differ most for alcohol pairs (1-6ol–1-8ol r 0.52 vs 0.32; 1-5ol–1-8ol 0.44 vs 0.32).
    • aa's row is nearly identical, since in both it comes from the same 4 flies.
    • kc_remy is slightly less claw-like: r 0.81 vs 0.84 with the static claw matrix.
  • What was re-run. Every somata-dependent analysis, with only the somata column changed (SOMA_COL=kc_remy).

Verdict

Every conclusion holds. With kc_remy the somata effects during the odor are about 15–20% smaller and remain significant. Three details shift:

  • Hemibrain model. In the joint model it now keeps some weight next to somata: +0.19 (p 0.04), vs +0.13 (p 0.16). Somata stays the larger term (+0.33, p 0.0002).
  • Quadratic check. It is weaker: +0.27 (p 0.02), vs +0.38 (p 0.001).
  • Somata clusters. They become k = 5: {2h, IaA, pa}, {2-but, eb, ep}, {B-cit, Lin, aa, va}, {1-5ol, 1-6ol, 1-8ol, 6al, t2h} and {benz, ms}.
    • ORN also splits off {benz, ms}, so the ORN and somata clusterings overlap more (ARI 0.11 vs 0.01).
    • Claw fly 3's early clusters match the somata more strongly (+0.30, p 0.004, vs +0.17, p 0.04).
    • The early → late rise toward somata still holds in 4/4 flies.

5 · Statistical methods

  • Why Pearson r between population vectors at each frame. At each frame, an odor's response is a vector with one entry per bouton or claw. Pearson r between two odors centres each vector on its mean across ROIs, scales it to unit SD, and takes the dot product: it measures whether the two odors drive the same ROIs more and the same ROIs less, and ignores response amplitude and any offset shared by all ROIs. That is the quantity the hypothesis is about (pattern similarity, not response size), it matches the static ORN and somata RDMs, and it keeps the same units in boutons and claws, so a slope of claw r on bouton r is the compression and residuals are interpretable (§3.8.2 gives the Spearman and Fisher-z checks). Its one systematic bias is attenuation by trial-to-trial noise: observed r = true r × √(reli·relj), with rel the same-odor single-trial correlation. The pair pattern is unaffected by this (raw and corrected agree at r = 0.99), but the compression magnitude is, so §3.2 reports both raw and disattenuated slopes; the analyses that compare pairs across regions use the reliability control described under pair movers.
  • Window matrices. Fly-mean matrices are the mean over frames of each fly's correlation-distance matrix, then the mean over flies. Windows are matched with a small time tolerance, because the PN-bouton time values carry floating-point drift. PN-bouton frames are linearly interpolated per fly onto the claws' 0.25 s frames when the regions are compared directly.
  • Odor-level inference. Each odor sits in 16 of the 136 pairs, so pairs are not independent:
    • p-values come from permuting odor labels (Mantel-style, or Freedman–Lane for partial coefficients);
    • uncertainty comes from the leave-one-odor-out jackknife;
    • independent fly subsets are used wherever noise could bias an estimate.
  • Split-fly IV.
    • Model: claws = a + b·boutons + c·reference, on z-scored pair vectors.
    • Boutons from one half of the PN-bouton flies serve as the regressor, instrumented by the other half (exactly identified two-stage least squares); c is averaged over all 20 splits.
    • Freedman–Lane: residuals of the reduced model are permuted by odor label, with the same permutations for every split.
    • For somata tests, both boutons and claws are instrumented by fly halves.
  • Clusters.
    • Average linkage on the correlation-distance matrix, with k chosen by silhouette (precomputed distances, k = 2–7) and labels from fcluster(maxclust).
    • ARI is from scikit-learn, with chance levels from 2,000–5,000 shuffles of reference labels.
    • Trial bootstrap: within each fly, trials are resampled per odor and the blockavg matrix rebuilt (1,000 draws).
  • Pair movers (§3.8).
    • Claws beyond E[claws | boutons]: z-scored claw similarity minus its least-squares linear prediction from z-scored same-time bouton similarity, across the 136 pairs.
    • Odor part: least-squares fit of rij = ai + aj, one value per odor. The pair part is the residual.
    • Reproducibility: the two halves of each of the 30 fly splits are correlated. For the pair part and the changes, odor labels of one half are permuted.
    • Temporal stability: cross-time split-half r divided by the geometric mean of the two same-time split-half r's, so noise doesn't count as change. SEs come from the leave-one-odor-out jackknife.
    • Window boundaries: the windows share their boundary frames (1.0 and 2.0 s). Half-open windows give stabilities of 0.87 (0.5–1 × 1–2 s), 0.96 (1–2 × 2–3 s) and 0.71 (0.5–1 × 2–3 s), and the same change reproducibility (0.46).
    • Reliability control: between-odor trial similarity divided by √(within-odor reliability of both odors), from the trial files.
    • Kinetic controls: boutons shifted by Δ, or low-passed with a causal exponential filter of the similarity time series (an approximation to filtering the responses), or several lags and filters together as regressors.
  • Software. Python 3; numpy, scipy, pandas, xarray, scikit-learn, matplotlib.

6 · Caveats and open questions

  • Small samples: 4 KC-claw flies and 5 PN-bouton flies, from different animals. Per-pair tests have little power; odor-level statistics are the reliable ones.
  • Static references: the ORN and somata matrices are static, from other animals and other response windows. Time-matched references could change the early/late picture in Figure 7D–F. Switching the somata matrix to the 4-fly kc_remy changes effect sizes by about 15–20% but no conclusion (§3.10).
  • Claw ROI mask unknown (§3.9). If soma ROIs are included, the claws' somata-likeness is partly built in.
  • Glomerular sampling: GH146 boutons are not the claws' full input. Differences in which glomeruli are sampled could produce claw-specific structure without any KC-level signal (§3.7).
  • The odor part rests on 17 odors. Its correlations with references (r ≈ 0.5–0.6) are only moderately significant (p 0.008–0.02). Its change over time isn't significantly directed toward connectivity (r 0.38, p 0.14).
  • The claw-vs-bouton relation is convex (§3.8.2). The linear residual, claws beyond E[claws | boutons], therefore carries a U-shaped component in bouton similarity. The conclusions hold under a quadratic fit, but 4 of the 11 marked movers, those at the high-similarity end, lose part of their gain to the curve.
  • After offset, claws outlast boutons. Claw RDMs after offset match bouton RDMs from about 0.75 s earlier. Post-offset claw-vs-bouton differences therefore mix kinetics (indicator or compartment) with reshaping.
  • Natural-source results depend on the VCF embedding. Raw VCF distances show no effect at any step.
  • chem_ecfp range. In the megamat17 table it runs from 0.42 to 2.0 (median 1.73), so it isn't a plain Tanimoto/Jaccard distance, which is bounded by 1. None of the correlations here are affected, but the metric should be confirmed before the Figure 6 Methods describe it.

7 · Suggestions for Figure 7 (and notes for Figure 6)

  • Show the per-frame time course (ARI and/or space correlations), or use an early window wider than one frame. The early effect sits in a single 0.25 s frame.
  • Report ARI with claws and references cut at the same k (e.g. k = 6, plus a range), not only silhouette-chosen k.
  • Add boutons as the control panel.
  • Soften "every fly showed a consistent shift with respect to both references": the ORN side holds in 3/4 flies, and only 2/4 are above chance early.
  • Defensible claw-specific statements:
    • Claw odor relationships depart from their bouton inputs toward the KC-somata (and connectome-model) structure from the earliest reliable time point.
    • At response onset, claw clusters are coarse, and the somata-like groups resolve within 0.25 s.
    • Both compartments decorrelate over the first second, claws about twice as much.
  • Temporal remapping (§3.8).
    • The somata-like pair structure is in claws from 0.5 s. What changes over the odor is the odor part (which odors are broadly similar), with odor-specific timing.
    • The odor-effects-by-window panel (§3.8, panel B) shows this compactly.
    • Don't interpret post-offset differences without the lag caveat.
  • If the manuscript switches to kc_remy:
    • take the somata numbers from §3.10 and 8_somata_reference_check/;
    • recompute Figure 6's somata statistics, which use kc_remy_combo and weren't part of this check.
  • State n = 5 PN-bouton flies for Figure 7 (one Table 1 fly excluded). Keep Figure 6 at 6 flies, or recompute it with the 5-fly column if consistency across figures matters more (§3.9).

8 · Reproducibility

  • Scripts: every result comes from the scripts in code/; code/README.md gives run order, inputs and outputs.
  • Re-run check: a final re-run on October 15 reproduced every CSV, JSON and PNG byte-for-byte; SVGs differ only in embedded metadata. See code/logs/output_checksums_after_rerun.txt. Steps 15–18 (§3.8), added that evening, also re-ran byte-for-byte, SVGs aside (code/logs/output_checksums_pair_movers.txt).
  • Somata column: the scripts now read the KC-somata column from SOMA_COL (default kc_remy_combo). With the default, every output re-ran byte-identical after the change (code/logs/somata_col_default_rerun_check.txt). §3.10 used SOMA_COL=kc_remy, with logs in code/logs/kc_remy/.
  • Independent checks:
    • a from-scratch recomputation by a separate agent matched the headline numbers to 3 dp (checks/independent_recompute.py);
    • an explicit two-stage regression matched the IV code exactly;
    • a hand-written ARI with scipy.cut_tree matched every cluster value;
    • a second from-scratch recomputation, of §3.8, matched to 3 dp. It covered the top pairs, odor values, split-half r, stabilities, change reproducibility, somata-cluster test and lag check. Permutation p differed only with the random seed (checks/independent_recompute_pair_movers.py).
  • Paths: the scripts use the Claude workspace's absolute paths. The README maps them to this folder; edit the D = … line to rerun locally.
